extracted.intended_audience: writers preparing submissions to literary agents and publishers (aspiring authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for authors preparing query letters, manuscripts, synopses, and ancillary materials to submit to literary agents and editors. Focuses on readiness, research, presentation, and professional practices across fiction, memoir, and nonfiction submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit only when manuscript is excellent / ready
rubrics_metrics.description: An impatient writer is a rejected writer. Don't query before your manuscript is as good as you can make it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agents seek excellence; excellence takes time. Wait weeks or months to tighten the work through revision rather than querying prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research agents via their online footprint
rubrics_metrics.description: Many, many agents are on Twitter. By reading their tweets, you can get a deeper understanding of what they seek as well as what kind of writing excites them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an agent's online footprint (tweets, blog interviews, website) to better target queries and to personalize query letters (e.g., referencing a specific tweet or title the agent liked).

rubrics_metrics.name: Write an excellent query letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't underestimate the value of an awesome query; some agents give a lot of weight to the query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get your query edited if needed, send different versions if you wish, and craft the pitch to 'suck in' the reader for fiction or emphasize platform/bio for nonfiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit a complete, fully revised manuscript (fiction and most memoirs)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fiction, the manuscript must be 100 percent complete before you send it. Most agents treat memoir submissions like novel submissions and want the full, edited memoir upfront.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are rare exceptions for memoir book proposals, but generally be prepared to submit the finished, revised book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nail your opening / make first pages compelling
rubrics_metrics.description: So many fiction submissions do not start in the most intriguing (best) place. There is immense pressure on your first pages to be great.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receive critical and blunt feedback; revise the opening so it hooks an agent immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and follow genre word count expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you submit, you should understand basic word count expectations; e.g., a 33,000-word 'novel' is actually a novella and often too short for agents to consider.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn standard word counts for your genre so you understand when and why to adhere or intentionally deviate from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctly identify your genre and age category
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand your genre before you submit; saying contradictory categories (e.g., 'women's fiction/sci-fi' or 'middle-grade/young adult/adult') comes off as amateurish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research distinctions (e.g., middle-grade vs. YA) and pick the category that best fits the book; crossover is possible but submissions should start from one clear category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't label the manuscript as 'my first novel' in queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Agents may discount 'first novels' as learning-experience works; avoid explicitly calling it your first novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the quality of the manuscript speak for itself rather than foregrounding inexperience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have independent critique / beta readers or a developmental editor
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you submit, you need an independent analysis of your work from talented, critical, honest readers or a freelance developmental editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise and overhaul your manuscript based on feedback so it's 'battle-tested' rather than a work in progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be part of a writing community / find your tribe
rubrics_metrics.description: Many successful debut writers are part of writing groups and communities, even online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate peers who will provide sustained critique and support as you prepare submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be able to succinctly pitch your story aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice describing your story to strangers in several sentences to force focus on main plot, characters, and conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps identify the most interesting and unique elements to highlight later in your query.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using prior self-publishing as a fallback for agent submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unwise and risky to self-publish just to see how it does and then plan to submit to agents if sales fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you self-publish, you'll have to disclose it and agents will wonder why it didn't sell; this can hurt your query's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the difference between pitch and synopsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Know that a pitch (back-cover style) and a synopsis (front-to-back summary) serve different functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare both forms appropriately: pitch to hook, synopsis to summarize plot and major beats; see guides for one-page and long-form synopses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always include a proper query letter (do not send only links)
rubrics_metrics.description: No matter what you are writing, you will need a query letter; do not try to skip this step and instead just send a hyperlink or attach your manuscript without a proper query.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the query to genre: novel queries focus on pitch/voice, nonfiction on platform/bio, picture book queries are short/cover-letter-like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test email formatting before sending queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Cutting and pasting text into the body of an email can lead to weird formatting issues and stray symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test-send queries to yourself/friends to ensure formatting appears correctly to recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be truthful and provide verifiable credentials
rubrics_metrics.description: If you mention previous publications, media appearances, or social media successes, be prepared for agents to verify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not exaggerate or fabricate; make sure there is an online means for verification (e.g., an embedded interview video).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain a simple online presence with contact info
rubrics_metrics.description: Have an online presence—even a simple one-page website with your name, head shot, and email address—so agents can find and contact you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do this even before publication or during querying; lack of an online footprint can mean missed opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study recent successful debuts in your genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Go to the bookstore and pick up debuts in your genre from the past two years to examine what they did successfully with pitches and first pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze back-cover copy and opening pages to learn effective ways to present your own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor agents' stated likes/dislikes for content sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow agents (e.g., on Twitter) where they often state specific things they will/won't consider (e.g., 'Please don't send me a book if there is a rape in the story').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these specifics to add or remove agents from your query list; respect agents' content boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Send queries yourself (do not have someone else send them)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not get someone else (relative or paid service) to send out your queries; sending a query email is effortless and should be done by you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions noted for disability. Having someone else send queries can confuse agents and create negative impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't query only one agent at a time (avoid exclusive querying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting queries exclusively to one agent at a time is a bad idea; it wastes time if that agent delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Query multiple agents rather than waiting months on one; the exception is if an agent explicitly requests an exclusive review for a limited time—understand the different senses of 'exclusive.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bookstore/Amazon and author sites to find comparable titles and agents
rubrics_metrics.description: If you're having trouble defining your book or who would represent it, scour bookstores and Amazon for comparable titles and visit author websites to see who repped them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparable titles (comps) to identify agents and refine your pitch/market positioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include both established and newer agents on your query list
rubrics_metrics.description: As you research agents, consider all agents who might consider your work—both established and new; newer agents are often actively seeking clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both types have advantages; don't ignore newer agents simply because they lack seniority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify that agents' preferences are current
rubrics_metrics.description: Just because an agent tweeted about wanting a type of book years ago doesn't mean that preference is still current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check updated guidelines on their website and recent public statements before querying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implying your manuscript has been unsuccessfully circulating for years
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not say the manuscript 'has been around for years' because that can suggest you've been submitting it with no success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such information may make an agent question why the book hasn't landed representation; strike a balance in describing a project's history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settle collaboration/ghostwriting agreements before seeking an agent
rubrics_metrics.description: Collaboration agreements with a ghostwriter, cowriter, or illustrating partner should be worked out in writing early on, before you seek an agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's not the agent's job to sort out coauthor or rights agreements; present a clean, agreed-upon authorship arrangement when querying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build platform before submitting prescriptive nonfiction
rubrics_metrics.description: For prescriptive nonfiction (not memoir or narrative nonfiction), you must have a platform when you submit your work or publishers will likely not consider the idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A platform includes blog/website, newsletter, public speaking, media contacts, social media numbers, and other elements that demonstrate your ability to market the book; platform-building should happen before publication.
